sentences.text: The great auk is the sole surviving species within the genus Pinguinus, a name derived from the Latin word for plump.
Adult individuals stood about 75 cm tall and weighed approximately 5 kg.
Their eggs were ovate and elongate, averaging 12.4 cm in length and 7.6 cm in width.
It is the only British bird recorded to have gone extinct in historical times.
Remains found near campfires prove Neanderthals used these birds as a food source over 100,000 years ago.
Artists carved images believed to depict the great auk into cave walls in Spain and Italy more than 35,000 years ago.
A specimen purchased in 1971 for £9000 holds the Guinness Book of Records title for the most expensive stuffed bird ever sold.
The great auk was declared extinct in 1852.
Charles d'Ecluse described the great auk as Mergus Americanus in 1605.
The great auk received its first official legal protection in 1553.
The great auk was an excellent swimmer that used its wings to propel itself underwater.
It could hold its breath for 15 minutes, which is longer than a seal.
The great auk primarily fed on fish like Atlantic menhaden and capelin, as well as crustaceans.
Its main diet consisted of fish, generally 12 to 20 cm in length and weighing 40 to 50 g, although it occasionally caught prey reaching up to half its own body length.
Remains from Funk Island suggest Atlantic menhaden and capelin were the great auk's favored prey.
Great auks formed lifelong mating pairs.
Great auks began their breeding pairing season in early to mid-May.
The great auk was closely related to the little auk or dovekie.
Some ornithologists still argue that the great auk should remain in the genus Alca.
Fossil evidence of the great auk dates from the Middle Pleistocene to the Holocene.
The great auk first appeared around 400,000 years ago.
Some researchers consider a 1852 report to be the last sighting of a great auk.
